notes.meaning: David calls on the "mighty" to give God the credit he deserves. Some take these to be angels in heaven. Others take them to be kings and great rulers on earth, who often keep the glory for themselves. No one can add anything to God. But we can openly say that all glory and strength belong to him, and the call is repeated because proud hearts are slow to do it.

God's "name" stands for who he has shown himself to be. Giving the glory due his name means giving him the honor he deserves, though we can never give him all he is worth. "The splendor of His holiness" may point to God's own holy beauty, to his holy house of worship, or to worshiping in a holy way. Older worship had fine buildings and robes. Now what matters most is a pure and holy heart.

Many think David wrote this psalm during a great thunderstorm. The "voice of the LORD" here is the thunder, which rolls from above where no one can control it. The "waters" are most likely the heavy storm clouds full of rain. The phrase "the voice of the LORD" comes seven times in the psalm, like peal after peal of thunder.

No sound in nature is as mighty and majestic as thunder. That makes it a fitting picture of God's voice. If God's voice is this strong, how great his hand must be! The storm should fill us with big, worshipful thoughts about God.

The cedars of Lebanon were the tallest and strongest trees people knew. Yet lightning splits them apart in a moment. If God can break such trees, people should not think their own power can stand against him.

In the crash of the storm, whole mountains seem to jump like young animals. This is a poet's picture of the ground seeming to shake during a great storm. Sirion is another name for Mount Hermon, a high mountain next to Lebanon. The "young wild ox" was probably a kind of wild buffalo or antelope (older Bibles say "unicorn").

With each roll of thunder comes a flash of lightning. The word means God's voice "hews out" the flames, like chips flying from wood or stone. The lightning shoots wherever God sends it. Some early Christian writers saw a picture here of the tongues of fire at Pentecost.

The storm sweeps south from the northern mountains into the desert near Kadesh. A wilderness is a lonely, empty place where God might seem far away. Yet God's voice shakes even there. Low, empty places must hear God just as the high mountains do.

The storm bends the oaks and tears the leaves and branches from the forests (older Bibles say it makes deer give birth early from fear). Meanwhile, in God's temple, everyone cries "Glory!" This may be the angels in heaven answering the call of verse 1, or God's people praising him on earth. While the world trembles, God's people worship.

The word for "flood" is used elsewhere only for Noah's flood. God sat as judge over that flood, and he still rules, holding the waters back as he promised. Some also see the heavy rains of this storm here. Either way, God is calm and in charge over the wildest waters, and he reigns as King forever.

The same mighty God gives his own people strength to serve him and to stand against evil. He also blesses them with peace. The psalm begins with glory in heaven and ends with peace on earth. After the storm comes calm for those who belong to him.
